thread:
Maya A: Quick question — trying to capture an nsys trace that shows kernel selection + KV cache behavior. I want cuda timelines, NVTX brackets around batching, and OS thread sampling to catch stalls. Observed a regression after a kernel-switch change; long tail on multihead_attn_kernel + kv_retrieval_kernel. Any recommended flags?
Liam H: Use --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt as a start. Add sampling so you see OS-level stalls: --sample=cpu. Keep the capture short but include warmup: ~25-40s. Also set --output to a directory so qdrep/qdlog stay organized. :thumbsup:
Arjun K: NVTX bracketing is huge here. Wrap the batch dispatch + KV lookup with nvtx ranges (inference_start/inference_end) and use --capture-range=nvtx:inference_start:inference_end to cut noise/file size. If kernel selection happens at a decision point, annotate that too (nvtx:select_kernel_start:select_kernel_end).
Ryan P: When comparing two builds, be sure to seed same input streams and run deterministic small batches (e.g., batch=1/2) so kernel heuristics pick the same paths. Otherwise sampling will be misleading.
Maya A: Example command you all recommend?
Liam H: Example I use for this kind of hunt:
```
nsys profile --output /tmp/nsys/run_kv_probe --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --capture-range=nvtx:inference_start:inference_end --duration=35 --force-overwrite
```
Liam H: Optional: add --capture-child-processes=true if your runtime spawns helper procs. If file size is huge, run with --export=sqlite for smaller parsing or use --output-format=qdrep and then convert.
Arjun K: For sampling interval tuning: start with default sampling and lower it if you miss short stalls. I've used --sample-interval=500us to capture sub-ms OS scheduling hiccups that align with KV evictions. But beware file size.
Maya A: How do you correlate the KV stall to a kernel? I saw a long time in CPU threads right before cutlass_gemm started.
Ryan P: Look for a CPU thread doing memmove/deserialize/kv-miss work in the thread timeline; then check adjacent CUDA kernels. Use the timeline view: select the CPU range and hit "Analyze with NVTX" to jump to NVTX markers, then inspect CUDA kernel launched right after. Often you'll see a big gap between host enqueue and kernel start.
perf-bot: saved trace to /tmp/nsys/run_kv_probe.qdrep (size=860MB) — use nsys-ui to open or convert to chrome trace: nsys export --output /tmp/nsys/run_kv_probe.json /tmp/nsys/run_kv_probe.qdrep
Maya A: Noted. Any tips for kernel-selection diffs? The new selector picks cutlass_fused_gemm on long seqs and perf reg is worse.
Liam H: Capture two runs back-to-back with nvtx tags marking selector entry/exit. Then in the timeline look at kernel footprints and SM utilization. If one variant has lower occupancy or much larger launch overhead, you'll see lower sm_efficiency and higher latency. Also check memory-bound metrics with --cuda-memory-usage or add specific metrics: --metrics sm_efficiency,active_warps if you need them (may slow capture).
Arjun K: If metrics slow the run too much, do a narrow capture around the hot kernel with --capture-range=nvtx:kernel_hot_start:kernel_hot_end and collect metrics only for that tiny window.
Maya A: Awesome — I'll run the two captures with the nvtx selector brackets and share qdrep. Thanks all :eyes:
Liam H: FYI: when uploading traces to the shared perf bucket, gzip the exported json and include a short repro script + nvtx annotations so others can replay easily.
Ryan P: Also drop a short note about CPU affinity/warmup commands used. Small differences there change kernel choice heuristics.
Maya A: Will do.
